# A Japanese-authored surface-analysis memo places binwalk in the command set, with a worked extraction

source: S132 — https://qiita.com/gpmrh096/items/a4cd80f102611995cabc — §「binwalkコマンド」 and §「表層解析で使用するコマンド」, published 2024-09-05 — as fetched 2026-10-23
verified-at: 2026-10-23
recheck: 180d — `curl -fsSL https://qiita.com/gpmrh096/items/a4cd80f102611995cabc \| grep -c 'binwalk'` -> 8 (ran 2026-10-23)
ground: the firmware extraction and region-inspection axis; the Japanese-native command vocabulary

**Claim.** The memo's surface-analysis command set is `file`, `strings`, `grep`, OpenSSL
tools, `zip`/`unzip`, `gzip`/`gunzip`, `tar`, `upx`, `exiftool` and **binwalk** — and it
states binwalk's role in the author's own words: 「binwalkコマンドは、圧縮、アーカイブ、
パックによって、ファイル内に埋め込まれているファイルを確認したり取り出したりすることが
できるコマンドです。」 The worked example runs `binwalk -B` and then `binwalk -e` on an
image and reports a gzip member at offset 11962987.

**Why this matters for the lane.** The lane's firmware axis is anchored on unblob and
binwalk *upstream documentation* (wave 1 S106, S109). This row is the **native Japanese
practition** of the same step, and it is reproducible: a reader can run the same two flags
on the same kind of input and get the same class of output. It also shows the ordering a
practitioner uses — surface triage (file/strings/compression probes) *before* anything
heavier.

**Caveats.** A personal memo on a user blog platform: `community` kind, tier **B** only
because the commands and the worked output are reproducible. It is **not** authoritative
about binwalk's behaviour (the upstream README is), and the offset in the worked example
belongs to that particular input file, not to any general claim.
